To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The mathematical flexibility of college-aged students was low.
students are unable to think flexibly in math and the inability to think flexibly is unrelated to cognitive and affective math factors.

1) students are able to generate a small number of unique strategies beyond the one taught in school, 2) math anxiety, math self-concept, need for cognition and working memory are not related to flexible thinking, and 3) students' beliefs about how many solutions exist are related to flexible thinking
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mathematical flexibility of students who have completed their K 14 education in the United State.
how people reason about mathematics.
the development of flexible mathematical thinking, and how students’ beliefs about mathematics and their own ability to think mathematically may affect their mathematical flexibility.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mathematical flexibility of undergraduate students who completed their k12 education in the united states is limited and is not related to cognitive factors.
the mathematical flexibility of U.S. college students is limited by the traditional instruction that they have received.
the mathematical flexibility of students is related to how many possible solutions they believe exist, and not to any cognitive or affective factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
students may be taught a single way of solving problems in math, but they are capable of thinking flexibly about math problems if they are given the chance.
students are not as flexible as we might expect, and the more they believe that there are many possible solutions, the more flexible they become.
math flexibility is not just the result of cognitive processes, but also the result of affective factors and beliefs about the nature of math.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the way we currently teach math may be limiting students’ ability to think flexibly.
the way students are taught in school may make it difficult for them to think flexibly.
math instruction needs to be more flexible in order to promote flexible thinking.
